Why a Sidebar Is Not an Article

By Dana Okonkwo | Monday, August 17, 2026

A documentation site carries its whole table of contents on every page. That is a deliberate and useful choice for a reader who arrived looking for one command and wants to see what else exists, but it has an awkward consequence for anything trying to decide, mechanically, which part of the page is the article. The navigation is long, it is made of real words, and it does not go away when the post is short.

Measuring the body as a share of the page therefore measures the wrong thing. A three paragraph release announcement on a site with a forty thousand character sidebar scores badly not because the extraction failed but because the furniture is large. A ten thousand word essay on the same site scores well. The score tracks the length of the table of contents, which is a property of the template rather than of the extraction, and it moves whenever the site adds a section.

The failure this causes is quiet, which is what makes it worth guarding against. Extraction succeeds, produces a perfectly good body, and then that body is discarded in favour of whatever the feed happened to carry, which is often two sentences and a link. The full page was on disk the entire time. Nothing logs an error, the article looks present, and the truncation is only discovered later by someone reading their own archive and finding a summary where an article should be.

So the absolute length of the extracted text has to be able to settle the question on its own. Past a couple of thousand characters, prose is prose. The share of the page it occupies stops being evidence about anything, and insisting on it trades a rare false accept for a common false reject.

The rare case is also the recoverable one. Because the original page is kept rather than discarded after extraction, a body that turns out to be a fragment can be extracted again later with better heuristics, and the improvement reaches the whole archive rather than only what arrives afterwards. A body that was thrown away in favour of a feed summary cannot be recovered at all without fetching the page again, and by then the site may be gone.

None of this argues for removing the share test. A short run of text that happens to sit on a sparse page really can be a cookie notice or a navigation shell, and there the share of the page is the only signal available. The test earns its place exactly where the absolute length leaves the question open, and nowhere else.
